list.listitem: Active spondylolysis is almost exclusive to adolescent athletes. Spondylolysis should be suspected in any teen with focal low back pain. C

The best investigation for confirming the diagnosis in patients with low back pain is computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should be considered in case of suspected associated neural compression or in children and adolescents. C
Usual course of treatment is conservative. C
Patients with persistent symptoms may benefit from a Boston brace, C physical therapy, external stimulation, or, in rare cases, surgery. C

For adults with degenerative spondylolisthesis, alternatives that should be employed prior to considering surgery include non-narcotic and narcotic pain medications, injection therapy, and physical therapy. C
For degenerative spondylolisthesis, surgical therapy appears to be superior to non-surgical therapy; evidence for the addition of fusion is inconsistent. C

background.definition: Spondylolysis is an anatomic defect of the pars interarticularis, without displacement of the vertebral body. Spondylolisthesis is the forward translation of one vertebra in relation to the next inferior vertebra. It occurs most often in the fifth lumbar vertebra, although L4 spondylolysis is more likely to cause symptoms. Active spondylolysis is an acquired lesion in the pars interarticularis and is a common cause of low back pain in adolescents. Degenerative spondylolisthesis is a common cause of low back pain largely in older adults.

list.listitem: It affects 5% of children age 6 years and older.
It affects 3% to 6% of Caucasian adults.

Among elite athletes participating in high-risk sports (those involving axial rotation and hyperextension, such as gymnastics, dancing, baseball, football, soccer, wrestling, or weight lifting), 47% have spondylolysis.
Lumbar spondylolisthesis affects 11% of adults in the United States.
Repetitive loading of the lumbar spine in extension and rotation leads to microfracture in the pars interarticularis.
Congenital changes in lumbar vertebral bone may predispose to spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis.
Developmental spondylolisthesis results from inherited defects of the vertebral pars, facets, and disks.

Sacral anatomy may also have a direct influence on the progression of spondylolisthesis; a lower sacral table angle and higher sacral kyphosis were identified in children (between the ages of 6 and 20 years) with developmental L5-S1 spondylolisthesis compared with a control group; these differences may be predisposing factors for vertebral slip in developmental spondylolisthesis.
Acquired spondylolysis results from injury due to repetitive spinal loading and is thought to be a stress fracture.
The typical patient is an adolescent athlete who presents with focal low back pain, hyperlordotic posture, tight hamstrings, and restricted forward bending. C

For adults with degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis, the 2014 North American Spine Society guidelines state that standing plain radiographs, with or without oblique views, are the most appropriate, initial noninvasive test.C

The best investigation for confirming the diagnosis in patients with low back pain is computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should be considered in case of suspected associated neural compression or in children and adolescents. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Common in adults, rare in children, pain is usually worsened by lumbar flexion rather than extension and by sitting and radiates to the lower extremity; neurologic deficits may be present.
Common, characterized by diffuse spinal pain and tenderness in a person with significant lordosis.
Common, most often occurs at 10-35 years of age, characterized by night pain, responsive to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
Less common, consider in case of nocturnal and/or constant pain unaffected by activity.
Uncommon, most often occurs in young children, characterized by localized pain usually without radiation; signs of systemic infection can be present.

list.listitem: Spondylolysis occurs more often in adolescent athletes than in the general population and is more likely to be symptomatic in this group.
The typical patient is an adolescent athlete who presents with focal low back pain; he or she also may have hyperlordotic posture, tight hamstrings, and restricted forward bending.
There are no validated physical examination findings for active spondylolysis.
The 1-legged hyperextension (stork) test, once thought to be of diagnostic value, is a poor predictor of active spondylolysis and should not be used as a diagnostic tool.

In patients with imaging evidence of degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis, clinical characteristics include only occasional back pain; chronic low back pain with or without radicular symptoms; radicular symptoms with or without neurologic deficit, with or without back pain; and intermittent neurogenic claudication.
Oblique lumbar spine radiographs may show sclerosis and elongation of the pars interarticularis (scotty dog sign), while lateral radiographs will usually show a defect in the pars.

The 2014 North American Spine Society (NASS) guideline on the diagnosis and treatment of adult isthmic spondylolisthesis state that standing plain radiographs, with or without oblique views, are the most appropriate, noninvasive test for detecting lumbar spondylolisthesis.

However, the 2021 NASS guideline on the diagnosis and treatment of low back pain state that there is insufficient evidence to assume that, if spondylosis is detected, it is the cause of the patient's low back pain. Therefore, routine radiographic findings of spondylosis should be interpreted with caution.

According to a consensus statement of the same guideline, if spondylosis is suspected and radiographic findings are inconclusive, Computed Tomography (CT) scans are the most reliable method to detect a pars interarticularis defect. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) should be considered in the presence of suspected associated neural compression.
In children and adolescents, MRI may be considered the preferred advanced imaging technique, as it does not expose the patient to radiation.
The 2021 NASS guideline committee found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against the use of single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) in the diagnosis of spondylolysis.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to management.
Initial treatment: relative rest with activity modification for 2 to 4 weeks. C
If unsuccessful, consider anti-lordotic Boston brace (also called thoracolumbosacral orthosis [TLSO]) worn 23 hours per day for 2 to 6 months, followed by physical therapy. C
Recalcitrant cases may need external electronic stimulation. C
Surgery is required in only about 10% of patients in referral populations.
Non-steroidal antinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may help alleviate pain.
A retrospective cohort study that adjusted for between group differences found no difference in any outcomes for patients who received epidural steroid injections.

Surgical treatment for spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis has generally been reserved for patients who fail to respond to conservative treatment. It is required in approximately 9% to 15% of patients in referral populations.

A systematic review identified 7 prospective comparative non-randomized studies with 228 procedures comparing reduction followed by fusion (RFF) or in situ fusion (ISF) in children and adolescents with high-grade spondylolisthesis. Both were judged to be effective, although there was no non-surgery comparator group; RFF was associated with a greater reduction in the slip angle and a lower likelihood of subsequent pseudoarthrosis (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.99). Patient satisfaction and complications did not differ between groups.

A review of guidelines concluded that surgical therapy was superior to non-surgical therapy, and that evidence for the addition of fusion is inconsistent. They also recommend minimally invasive surgery when feasible. Alternatives to surgery include epidural steroid injections and transforaminal injections.

A RCT of surgery (decompressive laminectomy with or without fusion) compared with nonoperative care for degenerative spondylolisthesis showed no significant differences in treatment outcomes between the operative and nonoperative groups at 3 or 4 years. The authors believe that the ir findings were limited by nonadherence to the assigned treatment.

The conclusions of this and other reports of the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial (that combine the patients in the RCT with an observational cohort enrolled at the same time) indicate that surgery improves pain and some self-report functional outcomes, including in patients over age 80 years. There were no differences based on type of fusion surgery.

A trial randomized 267 adults with symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis and a spondylolisthesis of at least 3 mm at the level of the stenosis to decompression surgery alone or decompression with additional instrumented fusion. Decompression alone was non-inferior after 5 years.

A study randomized 321 adults with lumbar spinal stenosis and grade 1 degenerative spondylolisthesis to decompression plus lumbar facet arthroplasty or decompression with instrumented lumbar spinal fusion. After 2 years, patients in the lumbar facet arthroplasty had better outcomes.

However, authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs and 14 nonrandomized studies of surgery for lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis concluded that clinical outcomes, complications and need for reoperation were comparable for patients undergoing decompression alone compared to decompression and fusion; decompression alone was associated with shorter operation time, less intraoperative blood loss, and shorter hospital stay. A second more recent systematic review, also with 4 RCTs with 523 participants, concluded that adding instrumented fusion provided no clear benefit. While a third systematic review reported better outcomes by adding fusion to laminectomy, it included largely observational studies.

A systematic review identified 6 randomized trials with 2349 patients (dominated by a single trial with 2061 patients) comparing anterior lumbar interbody fusion with posterolateral fusion. Most outcomes including bleeding, operation time, and pain scores favoring anterior lumbar interbody fusion. This was confirmed by a second systematic review that had broader inclusion criteria.
Newer but less well studied are novel surgical therapies such as titanium 3-d printed cages and interbody implants.
For degenerative spondylolisthesis, alternatives that should be employed prior to considering surgery include non-narcotic and narcotic pain medications and physical therapy.
Relative rest with activity modification for a minimum of 2 to 4 weeks.

Anti-lordotic Boston brace worn 23 hours per day for 2 to 6 months, followed by physical therapy; 78% of patients had good or excellent results after wearing the modified Boston brace full time for 6 months, then weaning from it over the next 6 months. C
External electrical stimulation may be used for treatment of spondylolysis in recalcitrant cases. C
Physical therapy exercise interventions alone or in combination with other treatments have a positive effect on low back pain from spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis. C

In an RCT including 92 adults over age 50 with chronic low back pain and degenerative spondylolisthesis, flexion exercises are not inferior to stabilization exercises for the control of pain and improvements of disability.
Patients in whom symptoms persist for greater than 6 to 12 months may benefit from orthopedic and/or spine surgery referral.
Acute defects take 5 to 7 months to heal, and terminal defects may take 2 to 5 months. C
Progression of spondylolisthesis slows with each decade. C
In patients with childhood spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis, the incidence of back pain increases with age. C
Unilateral spondylolysis is not associated with spondylolisthesis or disability. C
For patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis there is a 10% reoperation rate. Risk factors for reoperation include obesity (OR = 1.9), comorbid diabetes (OR = 2.0), and tobacco use (OR = 1.5).

In a meta-analysis of observational studies of nonoperative care of children and young adults with spondylolysis and grade I spondylolisthesis, 83.9% of patients had a successful clinical outcome after at least 1 year. Bracing does not seem to influence success. Although lesions diagnosed in the acute stage were more likely to heal, most defects did not heal with nonoperative treatment suggesting that a successful clinical outcome does not depend on healing.

algorithm.title: Suspected Spondylolysis or Spondylolisthesis in Young Athletes.

cell.label: Low back pain in young athlete
Positive 1-legged hyperextension test (does not rule out active spondylolysis if negative) or abnormal AP/Lat/Oblique radiographs of lumbar spine.
Relative rest for at least 2-4 weeks, NSAIDs or acetaminophen for pain.
CT scan, consider MRI in case of associated neural compression or young age.
Consider bracing if still symptomatic after 2-4 weeks.
Return to play when pain free activity. If symptoms persist, consider referral.
